hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to prominent rounded, spherical, or circular objects positioned in the left foreground, characterized by a distinct convex curve or arc that separates the subject on the left from the background on the right. The activating objects vary widely in identity and material—ranging from metallic car wheels, stainless steel sieves, and analog clocks to organic forms like a wombat, chestnut, or amber bottle—appearing in explicit colors such as silver, gunmetal grey, black, dark brown, or deep amber. The backgrounds are equally diverse, including white tiles, light gray walls, blurred green grass, or desaturated blue, though a clear contrast at the curved boundary is typical. The activating feature is strictly lateralized, typically occupying the left 30–50% of the image width, with the curvature bulging towards the center or right. The neuron remains invariant to specific textures, lighting conditions (specular vs. diffuse), and object classes, provided the spatial configuration of a rounded form on the left is maintained.
